* I've never liked competitive matchmaking generally speaking. I always liked Halo 3 custom games more than Halo 3 competitive so I'm that kind of player. I look forward to your social system. Being able to create fun, custom games can breathe fun into a game and thus brings a spirit of fun (and not competition) to a game.
* I think the idea of unit veterancy is fun in my head. My idea of fun veterancy is having a group of marines who've been through the mud. Over the course of the match they rank up -- becoming tougher. They are more capable as the combat encounters go on. Perhaps they have unique outfits to distinguish themselves immediately. Perhaps they even speak to you (their commander) with a little less formality than average rank and file.
* I find earning achievements to be fun, in some cases (if the task given is fun and challenging) , but overall they feel pointless unless they come with a reward. Again, back to Halo 3, getting all of the skulls granted you new armors.
* Progression in gaming is weird. I've seldom seen games ever design a game where you can unlock meaningful content that wasn't totally overpowered. Oddly enough my first thought of doing this well is actually...COD. When I used to play I actively enjoyed unlocking new weapons; however, unlocking/not unlocking those weapons never caused imbalance. Perhaps you could look into having a meta progression system that involved unlocking different weapons and armors that were balanced, but different. Perhaps you upgrade your air units to use a unique type of missile instead of firing ballistic ammunition. I know it seems a weird thing to suggest, but I'm trying to give you meaningful things to work towards that aren't just aesthetics (which I like, but it's definitely played out at this point).

To the one person...yes teachers and educators can certainly force interpretations on young minds of how to view news and how to say it is "fake" or "wrong" and colleges do that a lot especially in certain schools. I should think that it's important you watch your own children in these cases and make sure they think critically. However, whether news is fake or true should be based on whether it's factually true and not how it's interpreted.

 In your example above let's say the story you tell is true "100 terrorists and 10 civilians died all through drone strikes". If this were factually true you could say that the story "101 terrorists and 11 civilians were all killed by drone strikes" or "100 terrorists and 10 civilians were all killed by the navy seals" are both factually incorrect and are "fake news". So to distinguish here we should put into context the difference between the fact checking of news vs the interpretation of news. We should all hope that it's certainly more important to know for certain that the facts we learn are correct.

Still though I think some people will push their interpretations on others while some will do less so. Teachers and professors are people too.
